Chuck Yeager. The test pilot who became the first to break the sound barrier, a watershed moment in aviation history that proved supersonic flight was possible and opened a new era of aeronautical exploration. On October fourteenth, nineteen forty-seven, Yeager flew the rocket-powered Bell X-One at forty-five thousand feet over the Mojave Desert, achieving Mach one point zero-seven and crossing the sound barrier by a narrow margin to ensure safe passage. He had broken two ribs the day before the flight but flew anyway, strapping himself in by hand. Yeager remained with the United States Air Force for decades, serving as a test pilot and instructor at Edwards Air Force Base. In nineteen fifty-three, he flew the X-1A to Mach two point four-four, becoming the first to exceed twice the speed of sound. In nineteen sixty-three, he survived ejecting from an F-104 Starfighter over China and was rescued by an American officer. Yeager became a cultural icon, featured prominently in Tom Wolfe's The Right Stuff and its film adaptation. He continued the tradition of test-piloting experimental aircraft established by Jimmy Doolittle and pursued innovations that resembled Howard Hughes' own record-setting ambitions.
